name: Xometry
tagline: Upload a CAD file, get an instant price for CNC machining, 3D printing, sheet metal, and injection molding, then have a vetted shop actually make it.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The web app is the thin part. What you are actually buying is a network of thousands of qualified machine shops, a pricing model trained on years of real quotes and real outcomes, and someone who owns the problem when a part comes back out of tolerance. An agent can absolutely build you a geometry-aware cost estimator that reads an STL and spits out a number, and that number will be plausible and occasionally useful for sanity-checking a vendor. It will not cut metal, it will not know that a 0.4mm internal fillet is unmachinable, and it will not ship you anything. Build the estimator if you quote parts often enough to want a gut check, but keep the account.
coreLoopDIY: Loads a local STL or OBJ, measures bounding box, volume, surface area, and stock removal, then applies your own configurable material and machine rates to produce a rough per-part and per-batch cost estimate.
requirements: Your own material and shop rate assumptions, which you have to source yourself
CAD exports in STL or OBJ; STEP parsing is a much bigger job
whatYouLose: The supplier network: your estimate has nobody to send the file to
Manufacturability feedback, thin walls, undercuts, tool access, draft angles, all the things that turn a cheap quote into a rejection
Real pricing calibrated on actual accepted jobs, not your guessed rates
Quality assurance, inspection reports, certifications, and a counterparty if the part is wrong
Logistics, lead time commitments, and ITAR or ISO-scoped handling
moatNotes: The instant quote is a pricing model on top of a supply network. Either half alone is worth much less than the pair.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the alternative is emailing six machine shops, waiting four days, and getting three replies with wildly different numbers and no way to compare them. Xometry collapses that into a price in a browser and a part on a dock, and it absorbs the risk of a shop missing spec. Engineers pay for the absence of procurement work, not for the quoting UI. A local estimator helps you argue about a quote; it does not help you get a part.
notes: The quote calculator is a weekend build; the thing on the other end of the quote is not. The moat is marketplace liquidity plus years of accepted-bid pricing data, and no amount of geometry math substitutes for a shop that will actually run the job.
prompt:
Build a local-only manufacturing cost estimator called "Quotebench". Single-user desktop web app, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + React + TypeScript
- three.js with STLLoader and OBJLoader for mesh parsing and preview
- Tailwind for styling
- Everything client-side; persist state in localStorage. No backend at all.

Core flow:
1. Drag an .stl or .obj file onto the page. Parse it in the browser.
2. Render the mesh in a three.js viewport with orbit controls and a 1cm reference grid.
3. Compute and display geometry: bounding box in mm, mesh volume via signed tetrahedron sum, surface area, triangle count, and a convex-hull-free estimate of required rectangular stock (bbox plus a configurable per-face allowance).
4. Let the user pick a process: CNC 3-axis, FDM, SLA, or SLS. Each process has its own editable rate card.
5. Let the user pick a material from an editable table with columns: name, density g/cm3, cost per kg, machinability factor.

Cost model, keep it explicit and visible:
- Material cost = stock volume (CNC) or part volume x infill factor (printing) x density x cost per kg, with a configurable scrap percentage.
- Machine time for CNC = (stock volume minus part volume) / configurable removal rate in cm3/min, divided by machinability factor.
- Machine time for printing = part volume / configurable deposition rate, plus layer-count overhead from Z height / layer height.
- Labor and setup = flat per-job fee plus per-part handling time.
- Total = material + machine time x machine rate + labor, then apply a quantity curve: configurable setup amortization across batch size.
- Show the full arithmetic as a line-item breakdown, not just a final number. Every coefficient is editable in a settings panel and persisted.

Also build:
- A saved parts list: name, file hash, geometry, chosen process, last estimate. Stored in localStorage.
- Quantity breaks table for 1, 10, 50, 100, 500 showing per-unit cost.
- Export a single quote as a printable HTML page via window.print, and the parts list as CSV.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt and do not stub with fake data:
- STEP or IGES parsing
- Manufacturability or DFM checks, tool access analysis, undercut detection
- Any supplier lookup, ordering, shipping, or network calls
- Real-world material prices; ship the rate card empty with a clear note that the user must enter their own numbers

Include a README that says in plain language: this estimates, it does not quote, and the numbers are only as good as the rate card you type in.
No .env needed since there are no secrets and no services.
